title: CS Quest 1.4 · Counting and remembering (Variables)
name: Counting and remembering (Variables)
summary: Students create variables with names a partner can read, in three types: a number like count, an on/off flag like hasKey, and a word from a list like color. In Robo Route the shelf offers good and bad names and the level refuses x or thing and says why; the last level is a working program that nobody can read until it is renamed. One device per student.
iCan: name a variable so a partner knows what it holds
choose the type that fits: a number, an on/off flag, or a word
set a variable and change it with an operation as the program runs
materials: Variable Jars printable (jar labels, counters, set and change cards, a variables table)
doNow: Think of the score in your favorite game. What makes it go up? What makes it go down? Now name two more things the game must remember, and say whether each is a number, a yes/no, or a word.
plan: Explore: name it right on level 1, the three kinds of boxes

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 1.3, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 1.3

do: Open Robo Route at Variables on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Level 1 has seven gems up the left side and a door that opens when a box says 7. Build it the lazy way first: pick the name x from the shelf, set x to 0, repeat 7 with forward, pick up, change x by 1. Run it. The level refuses the name and says why. Rename to count and run again; read the watch pill as it climbs.

On the board draw three boxes and label them number, flag, word. Fill them from the game: count holds a number; hasKey is on or off; color holds a word from a list. Ask for one more example of each from the Do Now.
say: A variable is a labeled box the program can look in and change. The name is for the people who read the program: x says nothing, gemsLeft says everything.

Boxes come in types. A number box counts. A flag box is on or off. A word box holds one word from a list. Pick the type that fits what you store, and an operation that fits the type: you can add to a number, you cannot add to a flag.
ask: Why is x a bad name? Who pays for it?
explore.afterAsk: The partner who reads the program next, and you in a week. Then show level 6's idea: a program that works but nobody can read, and the only fix is renaming.
explore.bigIdea: A variable is a named box with a type; a clear name is for the people who read the program.

play.goal: 4 levels, so everyone meets the on/off flag
play.stretch: the chapter, then 3 stars; level 6 is a working program with a bad name: rename it so a partner can read it
play.solo: one device per student; levels 1-3 are number boxes with the name check, level 4 a flag, level 5 a word, level 6 the rename; a neighbor may read your program and say whether the names make sense, never touch your screen
lookFors: picking the first name on the shelf without reading it, then arguing with the verdict: ask them to read the reason it gives
set where change by was needed, so the box refills to 1 instead of counting up
on level 4, the flag never set on after the pick-up, so the door reads off even though Bolt holds the key
play.misconception: A short name is not a good name: x works for the computer but not for the person reading the program, so the clearest name wins even when it is longer.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Why is x a bad name? Who pays for it?
Level 4 used an on/off box and level 5 a word box. Why not make everything a number?
showMe: One student shows level 6 on the projector before and after the rename; the class reads each block aloud both times and votes on which version a partner could fix.

exit.sentencePrompt: Name one variable from today, say what type it is and how the program changes it, and why its name is a good one.
exit.frame: My variable ___ is a ___ (number, on/off or word). It starts at ___ and changes when ___. The name is good because ___.

rubric.line: Variables: clear names, types and operations
levels: Names a variable or a type, with no reason and no operation
Names a variable with its type and says either how the program changes it or why the name is clear
Names the variable, its type, its start value and the operation that changes it, and says who the clear name helps

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: the watch pill is always on; read-aloud reads the verdict when a name is refused
hint 1 reminds the student to set the box first and names a good name
the three-boxes drawing from Explore stays on the board
stretch: level 6 renamed in one pass with the best name for every block, then explain the choice
fill in a variables table for a neighbor's level 4 program: name, type, starts at, changes when

unpluggedTwin.title: Variable Jars, three types
materials: three jars per group: a number jar, a yes/no jar with a lid that is open or closed, a word jar with word slips
steps: One partner is the program and reads cards; the other is the computer and does exactly what each card says: set empties a jar and refills it, change by adds or takes away counters, set hasKey on opens the lid, set color blue drops in the blue slip. Say the value of every jar after every card.
Naming round: cover the labels and name the jars x, thing and number1. Hand the cards to a new partner and watch them guess which jar is which. Then relabel with names that say what the jar holds.
Type round: try to change color by 1, or add a counter to the yes/no jar. Talk about why the operation does not fit the type.
Share: fill in the variables table for your three jars: name, type, starts at, changes when.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: think of the score in your favorite game, write one thing that makes it go up and one that makes it go down, then name two more things the game must remember and the type of each.

Play Robo Route, chapter Variables (Pro), one device each, for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 4 2 0 0. Goal: 4 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Why is x a bad name? Who pays for it?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut; in 5 minutes of Explore build level 1 once with x and once with count, and draw the three boxes while it runs

add: the Variable Jars, three types twin (15 minutes) before Play
the 3-star stretch and the variables table after Play
10 minutes of the Unit 1 review on Brain Board

notes: The name check is the lesson: the level refuses single letters and meaningless names and says why. Let students read the reason instead of telling them.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: value, set to, flag, operation.
One device per student at this band; the Standards tab counts each student's own play.

steps.body:

If the game asks for a quest code, it is 4 2 0 0.
Pick a name that says what the box holds. If the level refuses a name, read why. Set puts a value in; change by adds to a number box.
